summary: On 20 July 2015 Sentry's PostgreSQL database stopped accepting writes because it was running out of transaction IDs. Autovacuum had not kept up, and recovery took most of a working day.

overview.background: PostgreSQL numbers transactions with a 32-bit counter. To avoid wraparound, a process called vacuum must freeze old rows. If it falls behind and fewer than one million transactions remain, PostgreSQL stops accepting commands to protect data.
overview.impact: Sentry was down for most of the US working day on Monday 20 July 2015.
overview.severity: Full outage for writes, with reads served by replicas for part of the time. Sentry accepted data loss for one table to recover.
overview.gaps: The post does not quote the exact PostgreSQL error text, hardware before the incident or customer numbers.

archNote: The primary, replicas and table are described in the post. The picture is simplified.

timeline.e: Autovacuum settings were left at values too slow for the write load, and autovacuum logging was not verbose.
PostgreSQL stops accepting commands because fewer than one million transaction IDs remain.
Writes are stopped and replicas serve reads. A failover to new hardware is prepared.
The team waits on autovacuum and then finds that one large table has not finished.
The unfinished table is truncated, accepting data loss for that table.
New autovacuum settings are applied on new hardware with 256 GB memory and 24 cores.

rootCause.trigger: The database consumed transaction IDs until fewer than one million remained.
rootCause.underlying: Autovacuum could not freeze old rows fast enough because its limits were conservative for the workload.
contributing: Only the default three workers ran
One vacuum failed or did not work and nobody was alerted
Autovacuum logging was not verbose enough to see it
propagation: The ID counter nears its limit.

diagnose.step: Check how close each database is to the limit.
diagnose.cmd: SELECT datname, age(datfrozenxid) FROM pg_database ORDER BY 2 DESC;
SELECT relname, age(relfrozenxid) FROM pg_class WHERE relkind='r' ORDER BY 2 DESC LIMIT 10;

diagnose.step: See whether autovacuum is running or stuck.
diagnose.why: Sentry found one vacuum had failed or not worked.
diagnose.cmd: SELECT pid, query, now() - query_start AS running FROM pg_stat_activity WHERE query LIKE 'autovacuum%';

correct.step: Stop writes and let vacuum work.
correct.why: No new transactions use IDs while vacuum catches up.

correct.step: Run a manual freeze vacuum on the oldest tables, with cost delay disabled.
As a last resort, drop or truncate a table that cannot finish and can be rebuilt.
correct.why: Sentry truncated one table and recovered in about five minutes. This loses data.

prevent.step: Raise the number of workers, shorten the wait and lower cost delay.
Alert when transaction age passes a threshold such as half the limit.
Split very large relations across databases.

fix.safety: Truncating a table is destructive. Take a backup first if possible and confirm the data can be rebuilt. Changing vacuum settings raises disk and CPU use, so watch load.

troubleshoot.scenario: Your database refuses writes. Reads still work from replicas. The logs say the database must be vacuumed.
clues: Transaction age is near its maximum
troubleshoot.question: What is your step by step plan?
troubleshoot.answer: Stop writes, keep reads on replicas, check transaction age per table, run manual freeze vacuum on the oldest tables with no cost delay, and if one table cannot finish and is rebuildable, consider truncating it.

options: Fewer than one million transaction IDs remained because vacuum fell behind

remediation.task: Write an alert for transaction ID age.
remediation.answer: Alert when age(datfrozenxid) passes about half of autovacuum_freeze_max_age margin, and page when it reaches a few hundred million below the hard limit.

remediation.task: Choose settings for a write-heavy server.
remediation.answer: More workers, short naptime, no cost delay on large servers, large maintenance memory within limits, and verbose logging.
Document what table, why the loss is acceptable, how to rebuild it, and who approves.

design.prompt: Design a Postgres setup that avoids wraparound surprises as writes grow.
design.answer: Partition or split large tables, tune autovacuum per table, alert on age, log vacuum, rehearse a freeze, and keep replicas and backups tested.

preventive: Tune autovacuum for your write rate
practices: Record what data you can afford to lose
